extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and current short-fiction authors, readers of Clarkesworld, and online SF/F editors interested in magazine metrics and editorial practices
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of the metrics, selection principles, and submission/process guidance an editor of an online science fiction & fantasy magazine uses to evaluate readership, submissions, and editorial choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readership measurement (unique readers & 6-month average)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The solid line in this chart indicates unique readers per issue and the dotted line is a cumulative six-month average that influences how I determine our monthly readership."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use unique readers per issue as the primary per-issue metric and smooth short-term volatility with a cumulative six-month average to inform how monthly readership is reported/understood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spikes as indicator of content resonance
rubrics_metrics.description: "One of the first things I notice when I look at this graph are the spikes and how they become more pronounced over time... If the size of a spike can help you guage the changes in potential market, the frequency should demonstrate interest in what the magazine has to offer."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large or frequent spikes are interpreted as evidence that particular pieces or issues resonated with readers (viral reach). Spikes are useful diagnostics of market interest but are considered side-effects rather than the primary editorial goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial selection goal: pick great content
rubrics_metrics.description: "When we select stories or articles, our goal is to pick great content. As far as we’re concerned, spikes happen when people think we met our goal. They are a side-effect, not the objective."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial decisions should prioritize intrinsic quality of the work. Popular reactions (spikes) are welcome validation but not the driving objective for selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shareability / viral nature as growth mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: "If you like something, you are more likely to share it. If someone shares something with you and you like it, you might just stick around and become a regular reader. In a sense, this is just good old-fashioned word-of-mouth marketing, but on steroids."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer content that readers are likely to share (strong hooks, emotionally or intellectually resonant pieces), since viral sharing is a primary mechanism for audience growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission intake and slush-pile process (online form since 2009)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Since 2009, I’ve been using an online submission form to collect stories from authors interested in being published in our magazine. These stories make up what is known as the ‘slush pile’... As you can see, we receive a lot more stories than we could ever publish."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain an online submission form and be prepared for a high volume of submissions; track monthly submission counts and rejection letters to manage workflow. Expect closure periods (e.g., holidays) that create dips to zero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission guidelines materially affect submission volume and types
rubrics_metrics.description: "The huge jump after the second reopening maps to a change in submission guidelines (allowing longer stories) and surge in readership and award nominations..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjusting guidelines (for example allowing longer stories) will change both the quantity and the kinds of submissions received; use guideline changes intentionally to shape the slush pile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance based on quality not submission volume or gender
rubrics_metrics.description: “Over the years, I’ve found it very interesting that the gender breakdown for accepted stories at any given period in our history is nearly evenly split, despite the wider disparity between the genders in the volume of submissions... In the end, quantity loses to quality.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection is driven by perceived talent and story quality rather than the number of submissions from any demographic group; aim for equitable outcomes by evaluating work on merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: International submissions profile and desire for translation diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: "The top eleven are shown... ninety other countries represent that ‘other’ wedge of the pie. I’m very pleased by the variety of countries represented... In the last year, however, we have had the pleasure of publishing two Chinese translations. This is an aspect of the magazine that I hope to see expand over the next few years..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track country-level submission data to understand geographic diversity; actively pursue and publish translations to increase international representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience demographic and platform statistics
rubrics_metrics.description:
"70% of our readers are in the USA
20% of our readers are in the UK, Canada or Australia
10% read from a total of over 30 different countries... 35% use an Apple computer
15% use Windows XP
5% use some form of Unix/Linux"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Profile readership by country and platform/OS to inform distribution choices, format targeting (e.g., EPUB/Kindle), and technical support decisions; recognize these are aggregate hints, not complete portraits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Podcast and audio-listen metrics as extension of reach
rubrics_metrics.description:
"Our most widely listened to story is also ‘The Things’ (17K+ listeners)
Roughly 5-6K of you listen to our stories on our podcast"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure audio listens separately from page reads to assess the magazine’s reach in podcast/audiobook formats and to prioritize audio production resources for high-demand stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social media follower metrics are a biased sample; use for advertising decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: "Obviously, this is more a profile of the 3500 people who are willing to follow us on Facebook (as opposed to the over 25K reading the magazine), but it does paint an interesting picture... in the end, it doesn’t influence us all that much though it might come in handy if someone decides they want to buy ad space from us."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat social-media follower demographics as a non-representative sample of core fans; avoid over-weighting these figures in editorial choices but leverage them when evaluating ad/audience-sponsorship opportunities.
